70_marg1038: The husbandman that laboureth, that is, the preacher, who in the field of the Church tills the hearts of the hearers with the hoe of the word of God. First partake, that is, take. Of the fruits, that is, the necessaries from the hearers, because “the labourer is worthy of his reward”; as the husbandman or vinedresser first tastes the first fruits of his labour, so the Apostle bids him who is first take first, and so distribute to the rest. For he ought first to supply his own need from what he has received, and afterwards minister to others from what remains. Thus he makes the chaste evangelist secure, one who does not preach the gospel in order to sell the gospel, and wishes him to understand that he may take necessaries for himself from those among whom he serves as a soldier of God, and whom, like a tiller, he works as a vineyard, or, like a shepherd, feeds as a flock. For it is not begging, but a right. Now Timothy was of such abstinence that, restraining himself even from things lawful, after the example of Paul he wished to live by the labour of his hands, although the Lord has decreed that he who preaches the gospel should live by the gospel.

70_marg1049: Saying that the resurrection is past already, etc. Or: so that it is understood of the resurrection of the soul. For there are two resurrections: the first is that which takes place in the soul through faith, when he who was dead in unbelief and other sins is made alive through faith and baptism, whence: “He that believeth in me shall pass from death to life.” The other is that of bodies, which will be on the day of judgment. The Apostle here speaks of that resurrection which takes place in the soul through faith, when he says: saying that the resurrection, of minds namely, has taken place in baptism and in faith, and that there will be no resurrection of bodies. All sects that profess religion grant the resurrection of minds in faith. For otherwise they would not seem worth hearing. Wishing therefore to be believed, even all who founded the sect of any false religion could not deny this resurrection of minds; all agreed about it. The number of such is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up,” a well of living water, a paradise with the fruits of apples. Of this number some live spiritually, and enter upon the more excellent way of charity. Others, still carnal, earnestly exercise their progress, and that they may become fit for the food of the spiritual, are nourished with the milk of the holy mysteries; and what in evil morals is manifest even to popular judgment, they avoid in the fear of God, and hold firmly the rule of faith diligently inquired into, and if they depart from it, are quickly corrected by catholic authority, although in its words, because of the carnal sense, they still waver amid various onsets of fancies. There are also some of that number who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the Gentiles, and yet even there the Lord knows who are his. For in that ineffable foreknowledge of God many who seem to be outside are within. Of all these, therefore, who, so to speak, are inwardly and in secret within, that is, whom the Lord knows, no one is led astray into eternal damnation. For the Lord knoweth who are his. For the judgment has not yet appeared, but it is already made in the knowledge of God. For he knows who will remain for the crown, and who for the flame; he knows the wheat and the chaff. For he says there will be such men as wish to be taught according to their own desires, so that they turn away from teachers who are steadfast and truthful to those who will teach them what they gladly hear, because the truth will seem harsh to them, so that, having left true doctrine, they give themselves to fables.
70_interl4151: by desire of hearing, yet not a good one
70_marg1073: Teachers with itching ears, etc. Augustine. On John, Homily 43. Solomon means these teachers by the woman, of whom he says: “The foolish woman and clamorous, and full of allurements, and knowing nothing at all, sat at the door of her house, ... calling to them that pass by: ... Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.” Though she is ignorant of the truth, she promises the knowledge of the truth, which by that very concealment she commends and, as it were, seasons, that it may be heard the more willingly. The seduced steal the hearing of it, which is forbidden. This concealment causes an itching in the ears of those who fornicate spiritually, as by the itching of lust in the flesh the integrity of chastity is corrupted. For wicked teachers by that very concealment season their poisons for the curious, so that they may think them to be saying something great because they have a secret, and may drink in more sweetly the folly which they think knowledge, and hear more pleasantly what is forbidden to be said and believed openly in the Church. That woman, on account of her unlawful and punishable secrets, is called not only foolish but also bold. For under the Christian name she has set up many wicked heresies, has fashioned abominable fables, and such dirges as are sung in the theatres are laughed at without hostile scurrility. And not such things as we grieve that such folly could have devised against God, and we marvel at its boldness.

70_marg1076: Delibor. We say libare: to taste, to pour out, or to sacrifice. Hence delibare, which however here is put for the sacrifice itself; for he calls his passion a delibation. For he is sacrificed to God who suffers for his justice.
70_interl4165: How do you know this? Because by the prevenient grace of God I have fulfilled what I owed. Or: I am about to depart soon, but I have fought the good fight, as if to say: I leave this example to you.
70_marg1077: I have run against the rebels, where the passage is easy. I have finished: the Church firmly established. In all things I have kept the faith, that others may do the same. He says this not as a thing fully accomplished, for there still remained the struggle of his own passion, but with firm hope, from the fact that the passion had been revealed to him; and therefore what he presumed would be, he declared as though done.
70_marg1078: The faith, which is the head of the Christian religion. I have kept: this cannot be had without God’s mercy, because it is the house of God; whence he says elsewhere: “I obtained the mercy of God,” not because I was faithful, but that I might be faithful. For we find that the Apostle obtained the grace of God without any good merits, indeed with many vices, the God who renders good for evil. He, as his passion now draws near, recalls his good merits, he who will obtain the crown the more, who after evil merits obtained grace, which, unless it had first been given freely, the crown would not be rendered. Therefore his merits are not his as though they were his own, that is, procured by himself for himself, but are gifts of God.
70_interl4169: which no one takes away; the same you too may hope for
70_marg1079: For if faith is grace, eternal life too is as a reward of faith. God seems indeed to render eternal life as a debt to the faithful man to whom he owes it, because he has deserved it through faith. But because faith is grace, and eternal life is grace for grace, therefore he will render it.

70_marg1080: The just judge, etc. Surely he is just in rendering good for good; yet he is first merciful in rendering good for evil, and that very justice by which good is rendered for good is not without mercy.

70_marg1082: The cloak was a consular garment, with which the Roman consuls were clothed when entering the senate house. Whence it is reported that the Romans had this custom, when they were gaining the monarchy of almost the whole world, that whatever nation met them with peace and crowns, they gave it freedom, so far that they were called their brothers, and were named Roman citizens. And they gave them power to build a senate house and to have consuls, as they themselves had. So the father of Paul, having been moved from the town of Gilohalum, where he had been born, to Tarsus in Cilicia, at a certain time when the Romans came through Cilicia, went out to meet them with the other men of Tarsus, as a noble, and they received them with peace. Then the Romans granted them the aforesaid things. And there Paul’s father received a cloak, and after his death Paul kept this garment for himself in memory of him.
70_marg1083: According to Haimo, this cloak was given to Paul’s father by the Romans as a mark of distinction, when he was received as an associate and a Roman citizen; whence Paul also calls himself a Roman citizen.
